summary: Describes the Stateless IP/ICMP Translation Algorithm, which translates IPv4 and IPv6 packet headers, including ICMP. It is a proposed standard, obsoletes RFC 2765, and was replaced by RFC 7915.

eli5.summary: A machine that rewrites the label on each packet between the old and new address styles, without remembering earlier packets.

questions: how does ipv4 to ipv6 translation work
what is the difference between stateless and stateful translation
how are icmp messages translated between ipv4 and ipv6
subtitle: How a translator rewrites IPv4 and IPv6 packet headers, including ICMP, without keeping per-connection state.

tldr.problem: A host with only an IPv4 address and a host with only an IPv6 address cannot talk directly, so something in between has to convert packets from one protocol version to the other.
tldr.mechanism: An IP/ICMP translator replaces the IPv4 header with an IPv6 header (or the reverse), maps the addresses algorithmically, translates ICMP messages, and fixes checksums, leaving the data unchanged.
tldr.outcome: RFC 6145 obsoleted RFC 2765 and has itself been obsoleted by RFC 7915, so it is not the current definition of the algorithm.

today: RFC 6145 is obsoleted by RFC 7915 and was updated by RFC 6791 and RFC 7757. It was a Proposed Standard that obsoleted RFC 2765.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
This document specifies the Stateless IP/ICMP Translation Algorithm (SIIT), which translates between IPv4 and IPv6 packet headers, including ICMP headers. It is the product of a 2008-2010 effort to define a replacement for NAT-PT, which had been made Historic. It derives directly from Erik Nordmark's SIIT in RFC 2765 and obsoletes it.

Readers are expected to know the framework in RFC 6144. Implementations MUST also support the address translation algorithms of RFC 6052 and MAY support stateful translation (RFC 6146). Compared with RFC 2765, this version moves the scenarios and the address format into those other documents, refines fragmentation and ICMP handling, and adds sections on IPv6 fragments and ICMPv6 Packet Too Big.

There are limits. The translator does not translate any IPv4 options, and does not translate IPv6 extension headers except the Fragment Header. Fragmented ICMP and ICMPv6 packets are not translated.
sections.eli5: This document is the instruction book for the translator. It says what the translator changes on each packet and what it throws away because the other side would not understand it.

sections.title: Translators and Stateless vs. Stateful Modes
sections.content:
The model has two or more network domains joined by one or more IP/ICMP translators (XLATs). A translator is a router: it must send a Packet Too Big error or fragment when a packet exceeds the next-hop MTU, decrement TTL or Hop Limit, and forward without translating if the destination is reachable by a more specific route.

In stateless mode, a specific IPv6 address range represents IPv4 systems (IPv4-converted addresses), and IPv6 systems have addresses (IPv4-translatable addresses) that map algorithmically to a subset of the provider's IPv4 addresses. There is no need for translation tables. In stateful mode, IPv6 systems may use any address outside that range, so a translation table binds their addresses to IPv4 addresses held in the translator. This RFC covers header translation for both, but leaves the stateful session database to RFC 6146.
sections.eli5: Stateless means the translator follows a rule that always turns one address into its partner, so it never has to remember anything. Stateful means it keeps a notebook of who is talking to whom.

sections.title: Translating the IP Headers
sections.content:
Going from IPv4 to IPv6, the IPv4 header is removed and replaced with an IPv6 header, the transport checksum is updated as needed, and the data is left unchanged. Key field rules:

  • Traffic Class is copied from the IPv4 TOS octet by default, and Flow Label is set to zero.
  • Next Header is copied from the IPv4 Protocol field, except ICMPv4 (1) becomes ICMPv6 (58).
  • Hop Limit comes from TTL, and the translator, as a router, MUST decrement it and check for zero.
  • Source and destination addresses are derived per RFC 6052. Packets with an illegal source address such as 0.0.0.0 SHOULD be silently dropped.
  • IPv4 options are ignored, but a packet with an unexpired source route option MUST be discarded.

Going from IPv6 to IPv4, the header fields are set as follows: Version 4, header length 5 (no options), TOS copied from Traffic Class, Total Length from the payload length plus the IPv4 header, and Time to Live derived from Hop Limit. Extension headers HOPOPT, Routing and Destination Options are skipped over, and the first other Next Header value becomes the IPv4 Protocol. A packet with a Routing header whose Segments Left is non-zero MUST NOT be translated.

Where the address mapping is not checksum neutral, the translator MUST recompute transport checksums for TCP and ICMP, and for UDP packets that have a checksum. Zero-checksum UDP needs a configurable choice: drop the packet, or calculate an IPv6 checksum. Translators MUST forward all transport protocols, even those they cannot fix checksums for.
sections.eli5: The translator peels off the old address label and sticks on a new one in the other style. It copies over the things that mean the same in both, like how many hops are left, and does not touch the contents.

sections.title: Translating ICMP Messages
sections.content:
ICMPv6, unlike ICMPv4, includes a pseudo-header in its checksum, so every translated ICMP message needs its checksum recalculated. All ICMP packets also MUST have their Type translated, and in error messages the embedded packet header MUST be translated too, which the translator does by running the same header logic on the inner header. It stops at the first embedded header and drops the packet if more are present.

Query messages with a counterpart are mapped: Echo Request and Reply (types 8 and 0) become types 128 and 129. Messages with no IPv6 equivalent or that are single-hop, such as Information, Timestamp, Address Mask, Router Advertisement, Router Solicitation, Redirect and IGMP, are silently dropped.

ICMPv4 Destination Unreachable (type 3) becomes ICMPv6 type 1, with the code mapped. Net and host unreachable become code 0, port unreachable becomes code 4, and the administratively prohibited codes become code 1. Code 4 (Fragmentation Needed) becomes Packet Too Big (type 2) with the MTU adjusted by the header size difference. Protocol Unreachable becomes a Parameter Problem. The reverse direction (section 5.2) mirrors this.

When the translator discards a packet it SHOULD be able to send an ICMPv4 error with Type 3 and Code 13 (Communication Administratively Prohibited), and an administrator SHOULD be able to configure whether such errors are sent, rate-limited or not sent.
sections.eli5: Error notes are like 'return to sender' stickers. The translator has to rewrite those stickers too, and also the copy of the original envelope stuck inside them, so the sender understands what went wrong.

sections.title: Fragmentation and Packet Too Big
sections.content:
IPv4 and IPv6 headers differ in size, 20 or more octets against 40 octets, so packet size matters. IPv6 routers never fragment, only the sender does, and an IPv6 link must carry at least 1280 bytes where the IPv4 limit is 68 bytes.

If an IPv4 packet has the Don't Fragment bit clear and would exceed 1280 bytes in IPv6, the translator SHOULD fragment it so each IPv6 fragment fits in 1280 bytes. IPv4 payload per fragment is then at most 1232 bytes (1280 minus 40 for the IPv6 header and 8 for the Fragment Header). If DF is set and the packet will not fit the next hop, the translator MUST send an ICMPv4 Fragmentation Needed error.

In the IPv6-to-IPv4 direction, a packet with a Fragment Header gets a cleared DF bit and the low-order 16 bits of the identification. Without a Fragment Header, the translator sets DF to one by default, which the RFC calls safer than causing IPv4 reassembly errors, though it may create PMTUD black holes.

Section 6 explains a field problem: studies found about 95% of IPv6 web servers responded correctly to a Packet Too Big with MTU 1280, but only 43% did so for an MTU below 1280. The workaround is for the translator to raise a too-small MTU in ICMPv4-to-ICMPv6 Packet Too Big messages to 1280, and, for packets of 1280 bytes or less without a Fragment Header, to clear DF and generate an identification value.
sections.eli5: IPv6 envelopes have a bigger label than IPv4 ones, so a full package might not fit after translation. The translator may cut a big package into smaller ones, or tell the sender to send smaller ones next time.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says stateless IP/ICMP translators introduce no new security issues beyond those in IPv4, IPv6 and the routing protocols used to bring packets to the translator. Deriving an IPv4 address from an IPv6 one can be risky for addresses like broadcast or loopback, and for non-translatable IPv6 addresses, but RFC 6052 deals with these.

As with IPv4-to-IPv4 NAT, the IPsec Authentication Header cannot be used across an IPv6-to-IPv4 translator. Tunnel mode ESP can be translated because it does not depend on header fields before the ESP header. Transport mode ESP will fail unless checksum-neutral addresses are used, and in both cases ESP endpoints will normally detect the translator and encapsulate ESP in UDP (RFC 3948).
sections.eli5: The translator does not open any new doors for trouble. But some kinds of sealed, signed envelopes cannot survive having their address label changed, so they need a special wrapping.

cells: Copied from Traffic Class by default
Derived from TTL, checked for zero
Derived from Hop Limit, checked for zero
Next Header copied; ICMPv6 (58) becomes ICMPv4 (1)
Fragment Header (44) added if DF clear or packet is a fragment
Fragment Header folded into the IPv4 header; DF cleared

items.label: Net / Host Unreachable
items.desc: Becomes ICMPv6 code 0, no route to destination.

items.label: Protocol Unreachable
items.desc: Becomes a Parameter Problem (Type 4, Code 1) pointing at the Next Header field.

items.label: Fragmentation Needed
items.desc: Becomes Packet Too Big (Type 2, Code 0) with the MTU adjusted.

items.label: Administratively prohibited
items.desc: Becomes ICMPv6 code 1, communication administratively prohibited.
